title: Brookfield Retail - model length, multilingual & toolchain evaluation
next_steps: Redwood to share hosted vs dedicated pricing worksheet
SE to run a 2-hour benchmark using Brookfield anonymized prompts (Priya)
Schedule technical deep-dive for infra team next Wednesday
action_items: Priya Nair - run latency/cost bench with 8k and 32k context prompts - due 2026-03-20
Jordan Reyes - share pricing worksheet and draft pilot SOW - due 2026-03-16
Evan Ortiz - provide sample traffic profile and VPC constraints - due 2026-03-17
summary: Intro discovery covering Brookfield's need for long context, multilingual inference, and tool-calling for POS reconciliation. Discussed tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments; open-model options and quantization; and initial pilot plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about 45 minutes blocked, really appreciate the time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Mark (Brookfield - CTO): Mark here.
[00:10] Lina (Brookfield - Head of AI): Lina here.
[00:12] Evan (Infra): Evan here.
[00:14] Sofia (Product): Sofia here.
[00:16] Priya (Redwood SE): Priya from Redwood. Amir also joining on the call.
[00:20] Amir (Redwood): hi all, thanks.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, quick agenda: understand your ingestion and prompts, discuss model options for multilingual and long context, tool-calling needs, and then map to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[00:30] Mark: Sounds good. To start, our main thing is customer support + realtime POS reconciliation, and we need model calls to handle order threads up to about 20k tokens, sometimes 30k for long invoices, also bilingual Spanish/English and occasional French. Latency target is sub 400ms for short reads, but up to 1.5s is okay for long coherence ops. Cost is a big factor.
[00:48] Priya: Helpful. When you say 20k-30k, is that full context passed every call or incremental KV cache you could manage?
[00:55] Lina: We could do prefixing for recent messages but we want the ability to resend full receipts and multi-file docs for a single session. For early pilots we expect to pass entire threads.
[01:05] Amir: That pushes us to models with 32k context or to implement a hybrid approach: prefix + retrieval + KV cache. Redwood's runtime supports automatic KV caching for repeated chat turns — but we'll dig into options.
[01:18] Evan: Security wise we need VPC and KMS, cannot send PII outside our network for pilot. At least until legal signs off.
[01:26] Jordan: Understandable. We typically propose Hosted for quick proof-of-value, Dedicated for predictable throughput and isolation, and Private for on-prem/VPC with KMS/HSM for regulated data. For PII-in-network constraints, Private is the safe bet.
[01:36] Mark: Cost-wise what's the delta between Dedicated and Private? If Private requires on-prem infra we need to factor in ops.
[01:42] Jordan: Right. Dedicated is a Redwood-managed isolated cluster in our cloud regions — you get reserved GPUs and SLA. Private adds a customer-managed control plane or on-prem footprint and higher setup cost. We'll share a pricing worksheet.
[01:54] Lina: Okay on models - we evaluated a couple internally: LLaMA-family forks, Mistral-like, and Falcon. We need good Spanish understanding for customer chat and also code-switching. Any recommendations?
[02:05] Priya: For multilingual with 32k, options are limited but some open models are coming online. Practically, you can look at Llama3 13B/70B variants (depending on your tolerance for hallucination), Mistral-instruct variants for cost-effective multilingual, and some patched Falcon derivatives. But there are tradeoffs: 4-bit quantized Llama3 can be cheaper but sometimes hurts instruction-following.
[02:28] Amir: Another pattern is to use a smaller multilingual model for NLU / routing / embeddings and a bigger context model only when you need long-coherence generation. That reduces cost. Redwood's routing can split requests by policy — e.g., short chats -> cheap model, long thread -> big 32k variant.
[02:43] Sofia: How does tool-calling fit in? We need model to call our inventory API to reconcile items automatically: so generate an API call, run it, and then patch the response back into the chat.
[02:53] Priya: Redwood supports function/tool calling. We surface a structured tool schema and can do deterministic tool invocation or allow model-first suggestions. For critical flows like payments or inventory updates, you can enforce allowed-tool policies and strong validation.
[03:08] Mark: Do open models support tool-calling reliably? We saw inconsistent behavior with some forks.
[03:14] Priya: It's growing but inconsistent across forks. Redwood adds a shim layer to normalize outputs and recommends a light middleware that verifies intents before side-effectful calls. Also watch for alignment settings — temperature and system prompt engineering help.
[03:25] Lina: We also need embeddings for search and retrieval for the prefix approach. Any advice on multilingual embeddings?
[03:31] Amir: Use a separate multilingual embedding model (like MTE-based or open models tuned for embeddings). Keep embeddings as a service — Redwood can host embeddings or you can self-host. Embedding vector size and recall requirements will affect storage and latency.
[03:42] Evan: On the infra side, traffic profile: peak 150 rps, typical 25rps. Most are short reads but heavy spikes during sales hours. Can Redwood autoscale?
[03:52] Jordan: Yes Dedicated clusters have autoscaling and burst policies; Private has options but depends on your infra. We can set SLOs and reserve burst capacity. For spikes, we recommend graceful degradation — e.g., fallback to smaller model or cached responses.
[04:05] Sofia: Any benchmarks on latency for 8k vs 32k context on dedicated GPUs?
[04:11] Priya: We have perf profiles — rough numbers: on A100-class GPUs a 7-8k pass might be sub-300ms for 13B quantized models with batching, but 32k windows on 70B variants push to 700-1200ms depending on batch sizes and kv-cache warmness. We'll run your exact prompts during the bench.
[04:31] Mark: That's useful. For the pilot, we want both scenarios: short 2-3 turn conversations and big doc summarization.
[04:39] Priya: Makes sense. We'll set up two benchmarks: (1) 8K-context Q&A for 1000 synthetic chats; (2) 32K summarization on 200 invoices. We'll measure latency, p95, token cost and failure rates.
[04:52] Evan: On encryption: KMS integration is mandatory. We use AWS KMS and a customer-managed key. Private must support this.
[04:58] Jordan: Redwood Private supports AWS KMS integration plus HSM for on-prem. We'll attach security docs.
[05:04] Lina: A few questions about model quality: we've seen hallucination issues when the model fabricates inventory matches. How do you mitigate that?
[05:12] Amir: Several levers: stronger retrieval and grounding, tool validation, lower temperature, and RLHF-tuned models help. Also can apply post-hoc verification: require the model to include sources or cite retrieval ids and then verify them against your DB before trusting.
[05:26] Mark: Do you recommend fine-tuning vs instruction-tuning vs retrieval-augmented prompting?
[05:31] Priya: For rapid iteration, retrieval-augmented + instruction prompts is fastest. Fine-tuning or LoRA on a model can improve domain accuracy but increases maintenance. We often start with prompt engineering + retrieval, then add LoRA or fine-tuning if necessary. Redwood supports pinned model versions and rollout controls for that lifecycle.
[05:48] Sofia: About multilingual - do we need separate models per language or single polyglot?
[05:53] Amir: Polyglot models are simpler operationally. However, in practice, some languages (e.g., Spanish) have better coverage on specific models; using a language classifier and routing can improve quality. Redwood's routing can have per-language policies.
[06:06] Evan: Any constraints about cold-start for KV cache? If a user jumps between devices we lose the KV?
[06:11] Priya: KV cache is in-memory and tied to session; for cross-device you should persist embeddings or a condensed summary and rehydrate cache. Redwood's platform offers prefix caching and stored summaries for that pattern.
[06:22] Mark: Ok, nuts and bolts — what pilot do you propose?
[06:26] Jordan: 6-week pilot: week 0-1 ingest and sync sample data (anonymized), week 2-3 run bench and tune prompts/model variants, week 4 user testing with tool-calling enabled on sandbox, week 5-6 iterate and produce SLO report. We'll propose costed options for Hosted quick start and Dedicated for pilot scale, with Private as option if legal blocks data exfil.
[06:47] Lina: Sounds reasonable. One more question: do you support streaming responses and partial tool results? We might want to stream a partial reconciliation result while aggregation completes.
[06:56] Priya: Yes streaming is supported. You can stream tokens and stream intermediate tool outputs. We also support chunked responses and patching an existing chat with tool outputs asynchronously.
[07:07] Sofia: Are there any gotchas with token accounting across multilingual inputs?
[07:11] Amir: Tokenizers differ by model; languages with multi-byte sequences may increase token counts. We'll measure effective token rates during bench so you get accurate cost projection.
[07:22] Mark: Ok terrific. I think that's most of our top-level concerns.
[07:26] Jordan: Great — quick recap of next steps: Jordan will send pricing and SOC2 + architecture; Priya will run two benches with your sample prompts and report back; Evan will send traffic profile and any VPC constraints. We'll schedule the infra deep-dive for next Wednesday at 10am.
[07:42] Evan: I'll send the traffic export and a short doc on our VPC peering limits.
[07:45] Lina: We'll anonymize a subset of chats for the bench by Friday.
[07:48] Jordan: Perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and materials.
[07:53] Mark: Thanks all.
[07:55] Amir: Thanks, bye.
notes: Call included standard sales discovery: context needs, model tradeoffs, security constraints, and explicit pilot plan. Minor transcription artifacts present (e.g., 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache' in a few spots).
